title: The Liking Gap
text:
After talking with someone new, many people replay the conversation and worry: did I say too much, did they find me dull? In 2018 Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney, Gillian Sandstrom and Margaret Clark measured how accurate those worries are.

In the lab, pairs of strangers had short getting-acquainted conversations. Afterward each person rated how much they liked their partner and how much they thought their partner liked them. Again and again, people underestimated how much they were liked. Their partners had enjoyed them more than they believed. The researchers called this the liking gap. It appeared in conversations of different lengths, and among people in a personal development workshop who talked in small groups.

They also followed first-year students at Yale who had just been assigned to live together as suitemates. The students rated how much they liked each suitemate and how much they thought each suitemate liked them, several times over the academic year. The liking gap persisted for months, shrinking only slowly. The researchers suggested that people are so busy monitoring their own performance in a conversation that they miss the clear signs of warmth coming from the other side.
lesson: The other person probably liked you more than you think. Let that knowledge make you braver about following up, reaching out again and being yourself.
people: Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney, Gillian Sandstrom, Margaret Clark
location: Yale University, New Haven, USA, and other sites
source: Boothby, E. J., Cooney, G., Sandstrom, G. M., and Clark, M. S. (2018). The liking gap in conversations: Do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742-1756.
